_about: Feature-length versions of live stories 11-20. Same rules as part 1: verified facts only; hedges from the research notes kept.

ida-b-wells.excerpt: She bit a conductor to keep her seat. More than 70 years before Rosa Parks.
sections: The ladies' car

Ida B. Wells was born into slavery in Holly Springs, Mississippi, in 1862. As a young teacher, she boarded a train in Tennessee and took her seat in the ladies' car. The conductor ordered her to move to the smoking car. She refused.

When he tried to drag her out, she fought back. In her own words, from her autobiography: "I fastened my teeth in the back of his hand." It took the conductor and two other men to remove her from the train. Most sources place the incident in 1884, one in 1883; the year is not stated here as certain.
Five hundred dollars, then nothing
Wells sued the railroad, and she won. The circuit court awarded her 500 dollars. Then the Tennessee Supreme Court reversed the decision.
So she picked up a pen. Wells became a journalist and co-owner of a Memphis newspaper, the Free Speech.
Memphis, 1892

In 1892 a mob in Memphis murdered the three Black men who owned the People's Grocery. Wells investigated and reported on the killings. A mob then destroyed the office of the Free Speech, and she could not return to Memphis.
Some accounts say the three men were her friends. That appears in only one of the sources we checked, so it is not stated here.
Chicago, and a prize 89 years late
From Chicago, Wells spent the rest of her life investigating and exposing lynching across the South. She died in 1931.
In May 2020, the Pulitzer Prize board awarded her a special citation for her reporting, eighty-nine years after her death. They took her seat, her newspaper and her city. Never her voice.

jack-johnson.excerpt: Champion of the world. Convicted over who he loved. Pardoned 72 years after he died.
sections: Galveston

Jack Johnson was born in Galveston, Texas, in 1878, to parents who had been enslaved. He fought his way up through boxing at a time when many white champions simply refused to fight Black challengers.
Sydney and Reno

On 26 December 1908, in Sydney, Australia, Johnson beat Tommy Burns and became the first Black heavyweight champion of the world. Many white Americans were furious. Newspapers and fans called for a "Great White Hope" to take the title back.

The former champion Jim Jeffries came out of retirement to try. On 4 July 1910, in Reno, Nevada, the two men met in what was billed as the "Fight of the Century". Johnson won. In the aftermath, white mobs attacked Black Americans in cities across the country.
The Mann Act

Johnson lived openly and refused to bow to anyone. His relationships with white women enraged many white Americans. In 1913 an all-white jury convicted him under the Mann Act, a law against taking women across state lines for "immoral purposes", in a prosecution aimed squarely at those relationships.
He fled the country and fought abroad for years. In 1920 he returned and served about ten months in the federal prison at Leavenworth.
The pardon
Jack Johnson died in a car crash in 1946. Sources give different dates for the crash, so none is given here; prize-money figures for his fights also differ between sources and are left out.

On 24 May 2018, seventy-two years after his death, the President of the United States granted him a posthumous pardon for the 1913 conviction, after years of calls from his family, lawmakers and boxing fans.

jesse-owens.excerpt: Four Olympic gold medals. Then he raced a horse, for money.
sections: J.C.

James Cleveland Owens was born on 12 September 1913 in Oakville, Alabama, the son of a sharecropper and the grandson of an enslaved man. When his family moved north to Cleveland, a teacher misheard his initials, "J.C.", as "Jesse". The name stayed with him for life.
Forty-five minutes in Ann Arbor

At Ohio State, Owens became one of the most remarkable athletes in America. On 25 May 1935, at the Big Ten championships in Ann Arbor, Michigan, he set three world records and tied a fourth, all within about 45 minutes. It is still called one of the greatest afternoons in the history of sport.
Berlin, 1936
In the summer of 1936, at the Olympic Games in Berlin, Jesse Owens won four gold medals: the 100 metres, the 200 metres, the long jump and the 4x100-metre relay.

A well-known story says his German rival Luz Long gave him advice in the long jump. That story is disputed, and it is not repeated here. Nor is the claim, found only in opinion columns, that President Roosevelt snubbed him on his return.
Racing a horse

When he came home, fame did not pay the bills. The world's most famous athlete still had to find a way to earn a living. On 26 December 1936, in Havana, Cuba, Owens ran a race against a horse, for money. For years afterwards he took part in paid exhibition races to support his family. How much he was paid for the Havana race is unverified; a quote often attributed to him about gold medals could not be checked against a primary source.
Recognition came slowly. In 1976, forty years after Berlin, President Gerald Ford awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Jesse Owens died on 31 March 1980.

major-taylor.excerpt: The fastest cyclist in the world, barred from most races because he was Black.
sections: Why 'Major'
Marshall Taylor was born in Indianapolis in 1878. As a boy he performed bicycle stunts outside a bike shop in a military uniform, and the nickname stuck: Major Taylor.
As a teenager he moved to Worcester, Massachusetts, expecting fairer treatment than he had found in Indiana.
Barred, boxed in, choked

Taylor was barred from most races because he was Black. When he did race, rivals used rough tactics, boxing him in on the track. On 23 September 1897, in Taunton, Massachusetts, a rider named William Becker choked him after a race.
Reports that spectators threw ice and nails, and that an Indianapolis track banned him after he set a record, come from a single source each and are not repeated here.
Montreal, 1899

In August 1899, in Montreal, Taylor won the world one-mile sprint championship. The Smithsonian and the Boston Globe call him the first African American world champion in any sport. The boxer George Dixon, a Black Canadian, had won a world title earlier, which is why the claim is worded that way. The Indiana State Library calls him "the fastest bicycle rider in the world".
He raced in Europe and won most of his races there. The number of world records he set differs between sources.
An unmarked grave
Major Taylor died in 1932 in the charity ward of Cook County Hospital in Chicago. He was buried in an unmarked grave.
In 1948, former cyclists, with money from Frank Schwinn, moved him to a proper grave with a marker.

mansa-musa.excerpt: In 1324, an African king brought so much gold to Egypt that gold itself lost value.
sections: The Empire of Mali

Mansa Musa, also known as Musa I, ruled the Empire of Mali in the early 1300s. Sources differ on his exact reign dates. His empire spread across West Africa, through parts of today's Mali, Senegal, the Gambia and Guinea, and it was one of the largest in the world at the time. Its wealth came from gold and salt.
The pilgrimage of 1324

In 1324 Mansa Musa set out across the Sahara on the pilgrimage to Mecca. Arab writers of the time described a caravan of tens of thousands of people; one report counted 60,000, including 12,000 enslaved attendants. His camels were said to carry 300 pounds of gold each.
Gold loses its value

When the caravan reached Cairo, Musa gave gold to the officials of the sultan's court, and his people bought, sold and exchanged gold freely in the markets. So much gold poured into the city that its value fell.

The historian al-Umari, writing about twelve years later, said that gold in Egypt had still not recovered its old price. That twelve-year figure comes from al-Umari alone, though Britannica and National Geographic both repeat it. A story that Musa refused to kiss the ground before the sultan also comes from al-Umari only and is not repeated here.
Timbuktu, and the Catalan Atlas
Musa brought architects and scholars back from his journey, among them al-Sahili, and built mosques in Timbuktu. The city grew into a major centre of Islamic learning.

In 1375 the mapmakers of the Catalan Atlas drew him enthroned, holding a nugget of gold. The drawing was made by a European who never saw him; it is not a likeness. His fortune cannot be measured, but seven hundred years later Mansa Musa is still called one of the richest people in history.

matthew-henson.excerpt: In 1909, he stood near the top of the world, and history almost forgot him.
sections: Cabin boy
Matthew Henson was born in Maryland in 1866. As a boy he went to sea as a cabin boy, and the ship's captain taught him to read and write.
In 1887, while working in a store in Washington, D.C., he met the explorer Robert Peary, who hired him. Sources describe the shop differently, as a hat shop or a clothing store.
Seven expeditions
Over the next two decades, Henson and Peary made seven expeditions to the Arctic together. Henson learned the Inuit language and became an expert dog-sled driver.
6 April 1909
On 6 April 1909, Peary's party claimed to have reached the North Pole. Henson was with him. Whether they reached the exact Pole is still debated.

Henson's own account says he arrived at the spot before Peary. That rests on his account alone, so it is not stated here as fact. A remark often attributed to Peary about how much he depended on Henson comes from a single magazine article and is not quoted.
Eighty years to catch up
Peary received the fame. Henson spent decades working as a clerk at the New York Customs House. Recognition came slowly: in 1937 the Explorers Club made him a member. He died in 1955.
In 1988 he was reburied at Arlington National Cemetery, near Peary. He had travelled to the top of the world; it took the country almost eighty years to honour him there.

muhammad-ali.excerpt: They took his title for saying no.
sections: Cassius Clay

He was born Cassius Clay in Louisville, Kentucky, in 1942. At 18 he won Olympic gold in Rome. In 1964, at 22, he beat Sonny Liston and became heavyweight champion of the world. That same year he joined the Nation of Islam and took the name Muhammad Ali.
Houston, 28 April 1967

In 1967, with the Vietnam War raging, Ali was drafted. On 28 April 1967, at the induction centre in Houston, his name was called. He did not step forward. He said his religious beliefs would not allow him to fight in the war.
The famous lines he is often quoted as saying about the war appear in different wordings in different sources, so none is quoted here.
Three and a half years

The punishment came fast. Boxing officials stripped him of his title and his licence to fight. In June 1967 a jury convicted him of draft evasion, and he was sentenced to five years in prison and a 10,000-dollar fine.
He stayed free while he appealed, but for about three and a half years, at the peak of his career, he was not allowed to box. He returned to the ring in 1970.
Eight to nothing
On 28 June 1971, the Supreme Court of the United States overturned his conviction. The vote was eight to nothing; Justice Thurgood Marshall did not take part in the case.
In 1974, in Kinshasa, Zaire, Ali beat George Foreman and became heavyweight champion of the world again. He died in 2016. They took his title. He took it back.

robert-smalls.excerpt: Before dawn on 13 May 1862, an enslaved man put on the captain's hat, took an armed Confederate steamer past Fort Sumter, and sailed his family to freedom.
sections: Beaufort and Charleston

Robert Smalls was born into slavery in Beaufort, South Carolina, on 5 April 1839. His mother, Lydia Polite, was enslaved too. When he was about twelve he was sent to Charleston and hired out: he lit the city’s street lamps and worked on the docks as a rigger and sailor, but most of his wages went to his owner. Year by year he learned the harbour, its tides, channels and sandbars, until he was doing the work of a pilot, a title the law would never give him.
In 1856 he married Hannah Jones, an enslaved woman who worked in Charleston hotels. He asked what it would cost to buy his wife and daughter: about 800 dollars. He had saved about 100.
The night of 12 May 1862

When the Civil War came, Smalls was the wheelman of the Confederate steamer Planter, an armed transport and dispatch boat that carried guns and supplies around Charleston harbour. On 12 May 1862 it took on four big guns from a dismantled fort. That evening the three white officers went ashore for the night, as they often did.

At about three in the morning the enslaved crew fired the boilers and slipped away from the wharf. They stopped at another wharf for their families, Hannah and the children among them. Sixteen people were now aboard; one historian counts seventeen. Smalls put on the captain’s straw hat and stood as the captain stood. At each fort he gave the expected whistle signal, and at about half past four they steamed past Fort Sumter itself.
A white bedsheet

Out of range, the crew pulled down the Confederate flag and raised a white bedsheet. In the morning fog the Union blockade ship USS Onward swung a gun toward the oncoming steamer and was about to fire when someone saw the white flag. Smalls handed over the Planter, its guns and its cargo, together with what he carried in his head: every channel, fort and mine in Charleston harbour. Within days Union forces used his information to take positions the Confederates had abandoned.

A line Smalls is said to have called out to the Union sailors appears in only one source and is not quoted here. The story that the crew had sworn to sink the ship rather than be captured is widely repeated, but we could not confirm it in two primary sources.
Fighting for the Union

Congress passed a bill to reward him and the crew, and Smalls received 1,500 dollars. The Union general in the region sent him to Washington with a message for President Lincoln and the Secretary of War: let Black men fight. Soon after, up to 5,000 Black soldiers were authorised for the area. Smalls piloted the Planter and the ironclad Keokuk in at least twelve engagements; in one battle, when the white captain lost his nerve under fire, Smalls took command and brought the ship to safety. He was then made the Planter’s captain.
Even as a hero he was not treated as an equal. In December 1864, in Philadelphia, he was thrown off a streetcar reserved for white passengers.
The house, and Congress

After the war Smalls went home to Beaufort and bought the house where he had been enslaved. He opened a store and a school for Black children, helped write South Carolina’s new constitution in 1868, and served in the state house and senate. In 1875 he took his seat in the U.S. House of Representatives, where he served five terms.

In 1895 South Carolina held a convention to write a constitution designed to strip Black men of the vote. Smalls was one of only six Black delegates and spoke against it. He lost that vote. He served as Collector of Customs at the port of Beaufort until 1913, and died on 23 February 1915, in the house where he had once been enslaved.

rosa-parks.excerpt: Her famous arrest photo isn't from that day.
sections: 1 December 1955
On 1 December 1955, in Montgomery, Alabama, Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a city bus to a white passenger. She was arrested.
The driver that evening was James Blake. Twelve years earlier, in 1943, the same driver had put her off his bus. She had avoided his buses ever since.
Not a tired seamstress
Rosa Parks was not simply a tired woman who happened to be in the wrong seat. She was the secretary of the Montgomery branch of the NAACP, and she had spent years working for civil rights.
Her arrest sparked the Montgomery bus boycott. For 381 days, Black residents refused to ride the city's buses.
The photograph
In February 1956, dozens of people, Parks among them, were indicted under an old Alabama anti-boycott law. She was arrested again, and on 22 February 1956 she was photographed being fingerprinted.

That is the picture most people know. It is often shown as if it came from her arrest on 1 December 1955. It did not; it was taken almost three months later. The date comes from the Smithsonian's National Portrait Gallery and the Library of Congress.
Browder v. Gayle, and after

In 1956, in Browder v. Gayle, the Supreme Court ruled that segregation on Montgomery's buses was unconstitutional. Her stand came at a cost. Parks struggled to find work, and in 1957 she and her husband moved to Detroit.
Rosa Parks died in 2005. In October of that year she became the first woman to lie in honor in the Rotunda of the United States Capitol. One seat. 381 days. A country changed.

sojourner-truth.excerpt: In 1828, a formerly enslaved mother sued a white man in a New York court. And she won.
sections: Isabella

She was born into slavery in Ulster County, New York, around 1797, and her name was Isabella. Her enslaver promised to free her a year before New York’s emancipation law took effect, then broke his word. So she walked away to freedom, by daylight, carrying her baby daughter. Sources differ on the year, 1826 or 1827.
The case for her son

Then she learned that her five-year-old son, Peter, had been sold illegally out of the state, to a man in Alabama. New York law banned selling enslaved people out of the state. In 1828 she took the case to court against the man responsible, Solomon Gedney. She won, and Peter was brought home to her. The court papers were rediscovered in the New York State Archives only a few years ago.

She is often described as the first Black woman to win a case against a white man. Sources word that claim in different ways, so it is not made here. The case itself is documented in the New York State Archives.
Sojourner Truth

In 1843 she gave herself a new name, Sojourner Truth, and travelled widely, preaching and speaking out against slavery and for women’s rights. In 1851 she spoke at a women’s rights convention in Akron, Ohio.

Her best-known speech, "Ain't I a Woman?", is also her most disputed. The version everyone quotes was published by Frances Gage in 1863, twelve years after the speech. An 1851 newspaper report by Marius Robinson, written at the time, does not contain the phrase. The National Park Service presents the famous text as disputed, and so do we.
Selling the shadow

In 1864 Truth sold small portrait cards of herself, captioned "I Sell the Shadow to Support the Substance". The shadow was the photograph; the substance was herself, and her work. That year she also met President Lincoln.
Sojourner Truth died in Battle Creek, Michigan, in 1883.
